title: The Borrowed Atlas
premise: In 1799, Tamsin Fairweather, an apprentice mapmaker of uncertain parentage, is completing the coastal atlas their murdered master died protecting when a stranger leaves a child at the workshop door with one instruction: forget the face. The child carries a hidden page — the true survey proving the Admiralty falsified the charts that wrecked the master's reputation and cost lives. To clear the master's name and give the child a future, Tamsin must smuggle the evidence past three checkpoints — the harbor, the customs house, and the Admiralty itself — before the century turns on New Year's Eve. They succeed at terrible cost, discovering along the way that the child is kin, and that belonging is not inherited but made.
about_author: Marguerite Vane is the pen name of a former archivist who spent years cataloguing nautical surveys in coastal England before turning to fiction. She writes about the people history forgot to label.

chapters.title: The Unfinished Coast
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Winter 1799: Tamsin works alone finishing the dead master's atlas, keeping hands busy and head down while creditors circle the workshop. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into meticulous labor, and the fear that the work will die unfinished.

chapters.title: A Knock After Midnight
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A cloaked stranger leaves a sleeping child on the doorstep with a note: forget the face. Inside the child's coat, Tamsin finds a folded survey page bearing the master's seal. Emotional beat: dread and reluctant responsibility.

chapters.title: What the Page Shows
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. By lamplight, Tamsin compares the smuggled page to the official atlas plates and realizes the Admiralty charts were falsified — sandbars moved, shoals erased. The master was killed for knowing. Emotional beat: cold clarity hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Child Who Won't Speak
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The child, roughly seven, communicates only through drawings — coastlines, a burning boat, a woman's face. Tamsin recognizes the handwriting style as the master's own. Emotional beat: tenderness breaking through self-protective distance.

chapters.title: Mrs. Quill's Ledger
chapters.summary: Mrs. Quill's POV. The landlady across the lane keeps accounts on everyone; she has noticed the extra mouth to feed and offers silence at a price. She suspects more than she says. Emotional beat: wary alliance between two keepers of secrets.

chapters.title: Checkpoint One: The Harbor
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin attempts to pass the evidence to a sympathetic ship's captain, but harbor watchmen — tipped by someone — search every departing vessel. Tamsin aborts, hiding the page inside an atlas plate. Emotional beat: first failure, sharpening stakes.

chapters.title: The Man from the Admiralty
chapters.summary: Lieutenant Harrow's POV. Harrow arrives politely asking after the late master's papers, all courtesy and threat. He notices ink stains on the child's sleeve. Emotional beat: the hunter's patience, and his own buried doubt about what he serves.

chapters.title: Apprentice No One
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Flashback woven through present: how Tamsin came to the master as a foundling apprentice, never legally claimed, always 'the apprentice.' The parallel with the child becomes unbearable. Emotional beat: identity as inheritance.

chapters.title: The Cartographer's Widow
chapters.summary: Widow Fairweather's POV (the master's sister). She arrives claiming family rights over the atlas and the child both. Tamsin suspects her motives but cannot prove them. Emotional beat: blood versus loyalty, and the question of who counts as family.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Two: The Customs House
chapters.summary: Mrs. Quill's POV. Mrs. Quill uses her ledger debts to bribe a customs clerk and moves the page through official channels — but the clerk copies it first. Emotional beat: uneasy triumph shadowed by new exposure.

chapters.title: The Copy
chapters.summary: Harrow's POV. Harrow receives the clerk's copy and now knows exactly what the evidence proves — and that his superiors ordered the falsification. He hesitates, then reports only partial findings. Emotional beat: complicity cracking.

chapters.title: Drawn in Charcoal
chapters.summary: The child's POV, rendered sparely. The child finally draws the whole truth: the wreck, the men who came for the master, and their own mother — the master's daughter, presumed lost at sea. Emotional beat: voiceless testimony becoming undeniable.

chapters.title: Blood and Ink
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Confronting the drawing, Tamsin realizes the child is the master's grandchild — and that Tamsin's own unknown origins may be tangled in the same household. Emotional beat: inheritance redefined as choice, not blood alone.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Lane
chapters.summary: Widow Fairweather's POV. The widow sells the child's location to Harrow to secure the atlas's copyright for herself. Mrs. Quill overhears and races to warn Tamsin. Emotional beat: betrayal arriving from the direction of family.

chapters.title: Flight Through the Fog
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin flees with the child through December fog, carrying the original page sewn into a coat lining, pursued toward the third checkpoint: the Admiralty building itself. Emotional beat: terror fused with fierce protectiveness.

chapters.title: An Enemy's Door
chapters.summary: Harrow's POV. Cornered, Tamsin makes a desperate gamble and appeals to Harrow directly. Harrow, holding the copy, must choose between career and conscience. Emotional beat: the unlikely door opening.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Three: The Admiralty
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. On December 30th, Harrow walks Tamsin past the guards under pretext of delivering maps. In the map room where the master once stood accused, Tamsin lays the true survey before the Board. Emotional beat: the small person standing in the large room.

chapters.title: The Century Turns
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs interwoven. As bells ring in 1800, the Board convenes an inquiry; the widow's claim collapses; Harrow submits his full report and resigns his commission. Emotional beat: reckoning arriving with the new century.

chapters.title: What the Inquiry Buried
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The Admiralty quietly settles — pensions, retractions, no public apology. The master's name is restored in the records but not the newspapers. Emotional beat: justice that satisfies and yet stings.

chapters.title: The Finished Atlas
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin completes the final plate and signs it not 'apprentice' but cartographer — then adds the child's charcoal coastline as a dedication page. Emotional beat: authorship claimed at last.

chapters.title: A Name for the Child
chapters.summary: Mrs. Quill's POV. The household settles into its strange new shape: Tamsin, the child, and Mrs. Quill next door. The child chooses a name for themselves. Emotional beat: belonging built rather than bestowed.

chapters.title: The Open Sea Chart
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, spring 1800. A letter arrives offering Tasmis—Tamsin—a commission to chart newly surveyed waters, the child to come along. Tamsin looks at the open horizon on the last unfinished map and begins to draw. Emotional beat: departure not as escape but as home carried forward.
